case_study_insert.main_stem: Quill & Reed Fashion (QRF) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Priya Quill, the business sells womenswear through its own website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. QRF plans to invest $620,000 in a new e-commerce fulfilment centre with automated garment sorting, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. QRF faces two problems: its online return rate has reached 14% and parcel-picking errors are rising as order volumes grow.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: An online survey of 800 shoppers found 58% prefer free returns and 47% would pay more for sustainably sourced womenswear. The website recorded 4,600 orders last quarter at a 14% return rate, down from 18% a year earlier. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. Customer complaints fell from 64 to 39 per month. The email launch campaign reached a 26% open rate and the mobile app conversion rate was 3.4%. A training needs review shows 18 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sorting machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $850 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Quill & Reed Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base rate from 3.75% to 4.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as QRF's $400,000 facility. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% to $14.20 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across QRF's workforce of 50. (3) Packaging and courier input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on online fashion grew just 1.2% and the sector's average return rate is 16%.

questions.question_text: QRF plans to fund part of its $620,000 fulfilment-centre investment with retained profit rather than the $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QRF of using retained profit in this way.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $220,000 carries no interest charges or monthly repayments, so it protects QRF's cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a 14% online return rate that ties up cash in returned stock. Every dollar not paid as loan interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in packaging and courier inputs, helping QRF hold its $38.00 selling price and stay competitive in online fashion without raising prices.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids the collateral and default risk of the $400,000 bank loan, so the new $620,000 fulfilment centre cannot be repossessed if the launch disappoints or the return rate stays at 14%. It also preserves Priya Quill's ownership and control: no lender can impose conditions on how the automated sorting operation is run, which suits QRF's flat structure and democratic leadership and leaves the founder free to redirect the $220,000 if customer demand shifts.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QRF's costs, return rate, financing mix and ownership.

questions.question_text: QRF is relaunching its womenswear range online. Consider a national television campaign, a social media influencer campaign, or the email launch campaign to existing customers. Which should QRF choose to promote the relaunch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: TV would build mass brand awareness quickly for QRF's womenswear across the whole country, which could support the $620,000 fulfilment centre by driving enough orders to use its capacity. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 50-employee online retailer, and most viewers do not shop QRF's niche sustainably sourced range, so much of the spend is wasted and it cannot be targeted at the 58% of surveyed shoppers who want free returns.

Social media influencer campaign: Fashion influencers can demonstrate fit and styling directly to engaged followers, matching the 47% of 800 surveyed shoppers who would pay more for sustainably sourced womenswear. Engagement is measurable and the creative cost is low. The drawbacks are slower brand building than TV, dependence on influencer credibility, and no guarantee of reaching the older shoppers who value free returns.

Email launch campaign to existing customers: With a 26% open rate already achieved and a 3.4% app conversion rate, email reuses QRF's own customer list at almost no media cost, converting proven buyers rather than cold prospects and limiting the 14% return rate because existing customers know the sizing.

Recommendation: QRF should choose the email launch campaign, supported by a modest influencer layer. Email is cheapest, already proven by the 26% open rate, and reaches customers most likely to convert and least likely to return items. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a business servicing a $400,000 loan; influencers alone are rejected as the primary channel because they cannot match email's proven conversion among QRF's own buyers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to QRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of QRF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of QRF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and influencer-only are rejected.

questions.question_text: QRF's parcel-picking errors are rising and its online return rate has reached 14%. Explain two benefits for QRF of using democratic leadership with its flat structure to improve performance in the fulfilment centre.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 50 warehouse staff to help design the picking routines for the new automated sorting machines, which raises job satisfaction and motivation (Maslow's social and esteem needs). Because staff handle parcels daily, their suggestions can cut the parcel-picking errors currently pushing QRF's return rate to 14%, protecting the $38.00 selling price from the cost of re-shipping returned garments.

Point 2: Involvement builds commitment and trust, which helps QRF in two ways. It supports the flat structure by pushing decisions to the workers closest to the problem, speeding up responses when order volumes grow, and it reduces the risk of staff leaving, avoiding the $850 per employee cost of off-the-job replacement training. Higher accuracy also protects the $620,000 fulfilment-centre investment by raising throughput toward the 20,000-unit output without adding fixed costs. Because QRF's structure is flat, these ideas reach decisions quickly, so improvements are not delayed by layers of management.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to QRF's errors, return rate, structure and costs.

questions.question_text: QRF must reduce parcel-picking errors among its 50 fulfilment staff. Consider on-the-job training on the new sorting machines or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should QRF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching staff beside the new sorting machines is directly relevant to QRF's own picking process, costs no course fees, and keeps the 50 employees productive while they learn, which protects the 20,000-unit output and helps tackle the 14% return rate immediately. However, the trainers are themselves production staff whose work slows, bad habits can be copied, and there is no recognised certificate, which may matter if the $620,000 fulfilment centre is audited by retail partners. Training on the actual machines also lets the 18 identified staff transfer skills immediately without a college-to-workplace gap.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $850 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a formal qualification for the 18 staff identified in the training needs review, costing $15,300 in total — small against the $620,000 investment. The weaknesses are that staff are removed from the line, cutting short-term capacity when errors are already high, and generic course content may not match QRF's exact sorting-machine settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: QRF should choose on-the-job training first, with short college modules later for senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while the 14% return rate is the urgent problem. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 18 of 50 staff from the fulfilment centre and spending $15,300 would damage the delivery schedule; college can be added once the new line is stable. QRF should review the 14% return rate and errors across the 4,600 quarterly orders after four weeks, keeping the college option open if accuracy has not improved.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to QRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of QRF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QRF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($38.00 − $14.00) = $180,000 ÷ $24.00 = 7,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 7,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38.00 − $14.00 = $24.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways QRF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 7,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 20,000 units to confirm the womenswear range is comfortably profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 12,500 units, which supports proceeding with the $620,000 fulfilment centre.
2. Use contribution per unit of $24.00 to model the cost of the 14% return rate: if one returned garment loses a unit's contribution, managers can quantify how much reducing returns to the sector's 16% benchmark or better protects profit.
3. Use fixed costs of $180,000 and contribution to set the volume target needed to service the $400,000 loan, checking that the new centre can cover its commitments before further spending.
4. Use labour productivity of 20,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 400 units per worker to benchmark the fulfilment centre quarter by quarter, linking accuracy improvements to the parcel-picking error problem and judging whether the automated sorters are working.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 7,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 20,000-unit output; contribution analysis of the 14% return rate; loan-service volume target for the $400,000 loan; and labour productivity of 400 units per worker to tackle picking errors.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QRF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has QRF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.54 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.92 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $185,000; 2025 current assets = $120,000 + $75,000 + $45,000 = $240,000. The 2024 figure is $185,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.54; the 2025 figure is $240,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.85. Excluding stock, 2024 liquid assets are $60,000 + $30,000 = $90,000, giving $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75; 2025 liquid assets are $75,000 + $45,000 = $120,000, giving $120,000 ÷ $130,000 = 0.92.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 1.54 to 1.85 rise means current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $30,000 to $45,000. The 0.75 to 0.92 improvement shows QRF is less dependent on selling inventory to pay debts, important while it services a $400,000 loan and funds a $620,000 expansion. However, trade receivables rose from $60,000 to $75,000, tying up cash; if customers pay late, these ratios could weaken quickly. Inventories also grew from $95,000 to $120,000, and with a 14% return rate some stock may be slow-moving, so the true quality of the asset base needs watching.

Conclusion: QRF's financial position has improved. Both measures rose, and the improvement in the stock-excluding measure shows it is not driven only by higher inventories. The main residual risk is rising receivables, so QRF should tighten credit control while going ahead with the fulfilment centre.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and cash movements and a justified conclusion on whether QRF's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QRF of offering free returns to its online womenswear customers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free returns directly matches the 58% of 800 surveyed shoppers who prefer them, so QRF can convert more browsers and build loyalty, which supports the $620,000 fulfilment-centre investment by driving the order volume needed to use its capacity. It also differentiates QRF from rivals and may help reduce the 14% return rate by encouraging customers to order their usual size with confidence rather than over-ordering.

Disadvantage: Free returns shift the cost of reverse shipping and restocking onto QRF, raising the effective cost of each sale beyond the $14.00 variable cost per unit and squeezing the $24.00 contribution if the 14% return rate persists. Handling returned garments also adds picking work at a time when parcel-picking errors are already rising, and returned womenswear may lose seasonal value, tying up the $120,000 of inventories shown in 2025 and worsening cash flow. Refunds also reduce the cash available to service the $400,000 loan and weaken the 1.85 current ratio shown in Appendix 2.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QRF's research, return rate, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 3.75% to 4.25%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in packaging and courier input costs will affect QRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.25%): If QRF's $400,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.50% of $400,000 = $2,000 a year (0.005 × $400,000). That is small next to fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about discretionary fashion and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but QRF can largely neutralise this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $14.20 per hour): With a workforce of 50, this rise feeds directly into the wage bill of the fulfilment centre and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The honest benchmark is the given productivity data: 20,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 400 units per worker. Only if productivity holds at 400 units or output grows can QRF absorb the wage rise without pushing unit labour cost up and eroding the $24.00 contribution per unit.

Input cost inflation (9.8% packaging and courier): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% that adds 9.8% × $14.00 = $1.37 per unit; at 20,000 units that is about $27,400 a year. Even a smaller effect on packaging alone would cut the $24.00 contribution, and QRF has only a limited ability to recover it because consumer spending on fashion grew just 1.2% and the sector return rate is 16%.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 20,000 units and directly erodes the $24.00 contribution that justifies the $620,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only about $2,000 and the wage rise can be offset if 400-unit productivity holds. Input inflation is rejected as smaller only if packaging is a tiny share of cost, which the insert does not state, so it must be treated as the largest risk.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to QRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QRF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of QRF with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
